The supported resource kinds are scripts and stylesheets.
Use stylesheet precedence to control relative cascade ordering.
gotchas: A stylesheet must provide `precedence`; omitting it makes the stylesheet configuration invalid.
Only preinit scripts whose immediate execution is acceptable should be used, because downloading completion triggers execution.
Preinitializing a stylesheet changes the document immediately rather than merely warming the cache.

preinitModule.summary: preinitModule tells the browser to fetch and evaluate an ESM module early. Use it when the module will soon be needed and immediate evaluation is acceptable.
preinitModule.explanation: Call preinitModule from react-dom with a module URL and an options object. The browser starts downloading the ESM module and evaluates it after downloading finishes. In server rendering, the call works only during component rendering or in an asynchronous context started by rendering.

parameters.name: href
parameters.description: The URL of the ESM module to download and execute.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: An object with required as: "script" and optional crossOrigin, integrity, nonce, and fetchPriority properties.

example.title: Preinitialize an ESM module
example.explanation: This starts fetching and evaluating the module while AppRoot renders.

useCases.title: Start loading during render
useCases.scenario: A component or its children will soon use a known ESM module.

useCases.title: Start loading from an event handler
useCases.scenario: A user action will lead to a page or state that needs the module.

useCases.title: Apply module effects early
useCases.scenario: The module must be evaluated as soon as it finishes downloading.

interview.question: What does preinitModule do?
interview.answer: preinitModule is a react-dom function that hints to the browser to fetch and evaluate an ESM module early. The module runs when downloading completes.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid immediate evaluation? Use preloadModule, which fetches the module without executing it immediately.

interview.question: What arguments does preinitModule accept?
interview.answer: href is the module URL. The required as option must be the string script; optional settings include CORS, integrity, nonce, and fetch priority.
interview.followUp: What values can fetchPriority use? It accepts auto, high, or low, with auto as the default.

interview.question: When does the call take effect?
interview.answer: In a browser, it can be called during rendering, in an Effect, or in an event handler. During server rendering, it only works during component rendering or an asynchronous context that came from rendering.
interview.followUp: Why call it in an event handler? Calling it before navigation or a state change starts loading sooner than waiting for the destination to render.

keyPoints: It gives the browser an early hint to download and execute the specified ESM module.
Evaluation starts after the module finishes downloading.
The options object must include as: "script".
Repeating the same module URL does not add another effect.
The function has no return value.
An event handler can begin loading before a navigation or state transition.
gotchas: Use preloadModule when downloading early is useful but immediate module evaluation is not wanted.
Use preinit for a non-ESM external script.
During server rendering, calls outside component rendering or its related asynchronous context have no effect.

preload.summary: `preload` from `react-dom` gives the browser an early hint to fetch a resource you expect to use. It can reduce waiting for fonts, stylesheets, images, scripts, and other supported resources.
preload.explanation: Call `preload` from `react-dom` to give the browser an early hint for a resource you expect to use. React can issue the hint during rendering or from other browser-side code, and repeated calls for the same resource are handled without creating duplicate equivalent hints.

parameters.name: href
parameters.description: URL of the resource to download.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Resource-hint options. `as` is required and identifies the resource type; `crossOrigin` selects the CORS policy.

example.title: Preload a font during rendering
example.explanation: This component hints to the browser to fetch the font while the page renders, before the stylesheet or text necessarily requires it.

useCases.title: Accelerate critical visual resources
useCases.scenario: A page is certain to need a font or stylesheet and should start fetching it before normal discovery.

useCases.title: Warm resources before navigation
useCases.scenario: A click will navigate to a screen that depends on external assets.

useCases.title: Announce descendant dependencies
useCases.scenario: A rendered component knows that its descendants will consume a specific image, script, or worker.

interview.question: What does React's `preload` function do?
interview.answer: `preload` is imported from `react-dom` and accepts a resource URL plus an options object. It gives the browser a hint to begin downloading the resource early, but returns no value.
interview.followUp: How would you preload an ESM module? Use `preloadModule` instead; use `preinitModule` when it should begin executing immediately.

interview.question: What are the required arguments and important options?
interview.answer: The `href` identifies the resource, and `options.as` tells the browser what kind of resource it is. `as` is required and supports resource categories such as `font`, `style`, `script`, `image`, and `worker.
interview.followUp: What additional option can affect cross-origin loading? Set `crossOrigin` to `anonymous` or `use-credentials`, as appropriate for the resource.

interview.question: When should an application call `preload`?
interview.answer: Call `preload` during rendering when the component or its children are certain to use the resource. You can also call it in an event handler before navigating to a page or state that will need the resource.
interview.followUp: Why preload from an event handler? It starts the fetch before the destination renders, giving the browser a head start.

keyPoints: Use `preload` to begin fetching an anticipated stylesheet, font, image, external script, or another supported resource before it is consumed.
It is a browser scheduling hint, not a guarantee that the resource will finish downloading before use.
Browser-side code may call it while rendering, inside an Effect, or from an event handler.
Rendering-time calls are useful when the current component tree definitely depends on the resource.
For anticipated navigation or state changes, trigger the hint from the initiating event to start earlier.
The function has no return value; its effect is the resource hint sent to the browser.
gotchas: `preload` downloads or begins fetching a resource; it does not start executing a script. Use `preinit` when immediate script execution is required.
Check the framework's resource-loading behavior before adding manual calls, because it may already manage these hints.

preloadModule.summary: preloadModule tells the browser to start downloading an ESM module early. It can reduce the wait when the module is needed later.
preloadModule.explanation: Call preloadModule to give the browser an early hint to download an ESM module. The browser can start the download while rendering or before a user transition. Use preinitModule when the module should also start executing immediately.

parameters.name: href
parameters.description: The module URL to download.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options for the module preload. It requires as: "script" and may include crossOrigin, integrity, nonce, and fetchPriority.

example.title: Preload an ESM module
example.explanation: This tells the browser to start downloading the ESM module before it is needed.

useCases.title: Preload during rendering
useCases.scenario: A component or one of its children will soon use a known ESM module.

useCases.title: Preload from an event handler
useCases.scenario: A button starts navigation or a workflow that will need a module.

useCases.title: Set fetch and security options
useCases.scenario: A module must be fetched with a CORS policy, integrity hash, CSP nonce, or fetch priority.

interview.question: What does preloadModule do?
interview.answer: preloadModule gives the browser a hint to begin downloading an ESM module early. It does not make the module execute immediately.
interview.followUp: How would you execute it immediately? Use preinitModule instead.

interview.question: How do you call preloadModule?
interview.answer: Import preloadModule from react-dom and call it with the module URL and { as: "script" }. The URL is the module to fetch.
interview.followUp: What must the as option be? It must be the string "script".

interview.question: When should preloadModule be called?
interview.answer: You can call it during rendering, in an Effect, or in an event handler in the browser. Calling it in an event handler before a navigation or state change can start the download earlier.
interview.followUp: What should you use for a non-ESM script? Use preload instead.

keyPoints: Use it when code expects to need an ESM module soon.
It starts a browser download hint; it does not itself execute the module.
Use crossOrigin to select the module's CORS policy.
Use integrity to verify the downloaded module with a cryptographic hash.
Use nonce when a strict Content Security Policy requires a trusted nonce.
fetchPriority can suggest auto, high, or low fetch priority.
gotchas: Calling it more than once with the same URL does not create an additional effect.
The options object must include as: "script".
On the server, it only has an effect in the documented server rendering context.

prerender.summary: `prerender` asynchronously generates static HTML for a React tree as a Web Stream. It waits for data required by Suspense before resolving, making it suitable for static site generation.
prerender.explanation: Call `prerender` from `react-dom/static` with a React tree and optional static-generation settings. It asynchronously produces a Web Stream containing HTML after data needed by Suspense has loaded; return that stream or consume it as required by the hosting environment.

parameters.name: reactNode
parameters.description: The React node to render as HTML, such as a JSX element representing the application or full document.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional static-generation settings, including bootstrap script paths and an abort signal.

prerender.returns: A Promise resolving to an object containing `prelude`, a Readable Web Stream of HTML, and `postponed`, an opaque JSON-serializable state when rendering is incomplete; otherwise `postponed` is null.

example.title: Prerender a static document
example.explanation: This server handler generates the complete static document as a Web Stream and includes the client bootstrap script so the browser can hydrate it.

useCases.title: Static site generation
useCases.scenario: Generate complete static pages at build time or on a server for static site generation.

useCases.title: Suspense-aware page generation
useCases.scenario: Render pages whose data dependencies are expressed with Suspense before emitting HTML.

useCases.title: Web-stream responses
useCases.scenario: Return HTML progressively through a Web Stream or materialize it as a string.

interview.question: What problem does `prerender` solve compared with `renderToString`?
interview.answer: `prerender` renders a React tree to static HTML through a Web Stream and returns a Promise. Unlike `renderToString`, it waits for all data to load before resolving, which makes it appropriate for static generation involving Suspense.
interview.followUp: How would you support a Node.js stream instead? Use `prerenderToNodeStream`, because the Web Stream API is not the matching output interface.

interview.question: What are the main inputs and output of `prerender`?
interview.answer: The first argument is the React node to render, while the optional second argument configures static generation, such as `bootstrapScripts`. The result is destructured asynchronously because the API returns a Promise.
interview.followUp: What should happen to the returned `prelude`? It can be sent in chunks as a Web Stream or read completely into a string before responding.

interview.question: How does prerendered HTML become interactive?
interview.answer: The server-generated markup must be hydrated on the client with `hydrateRoot` to become interactive. The bootstrap script option helps load the client-side JavaScript needed for that process.
interview.followUp: Why is `prerender` useful for static site generation? It waits for data before producing the static HTML, including data accessed through Suspense.

keyPoints: Import it from `react-dom/static` to produce static HTML through a Readable Web Stream.
Its primary role is static site generation rather than progressively streaming an actively loading page.
The returned Promise resolves only after required data has loaded.
It can generate complete pages whose content depends on Suspense-enabled data fetching.
The resulting stream supports either chunked responses or conversion to a complete HTML string.
Invoke the function on the server with the application root or document component.
gotchas: Use this API only in an environment that supports Web Streams; for Node.js, choose the Node.js stream counterpart instead.
Do not use `prerender` when your server integration requires a Node.js stream.
The generated HTML is not interactive until the client hydrates it.

prerenderToNodeStream.summary: Pre-renders a complete React tree to static HTML through a Node.js Stream. It waits for required data before resolving, making it useful for static site generation.
prerenderToNodeStream.explanation: Import the function from `react-dom/static` and await it with the complete React document plus optional streaming settings. It waits for data required by Suspense before resolving, then returns an HTML Node.js stream and optional postponed state; pipe the stream to a response or consume it as text. Hydrate the emitted markup on the client when interactivity is needed.
prerenderToNodeStream.syntax: const { prelude, postponed } = await prerenderToNodeStream(reactNode, options?)

parameters.name: reactNode
parameters.description: React node representing the complete document to render, such as `<App />`.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional object containing streaming settings such as `bootstrapScripts`, `maxHeadersLength`, and `namespaceURI`.

prerenderToNodeStream.returns: A Promise resolving to an object with `prelude`, a Node.js HTML stream, and `postponed`, an opaque JSON-serializable continuation state.

example.title: Pre-render an app to a Node.js stream
example.explanation: Pre-renders the complete app as static HTML and pipes the resulting Node.js stream to an HTTP response.

useCases.title: Static site generation
useCases.scenario: A Node.js server generates complete HTML files or responses during a build or request.

useCases.title: Streamed HTML delivery
useCases.scenario: A Node.js HTTP handler sends generated markup through a stream.

useCases.title: Resumable prerendering
useCases.scenario: A prerender is interrupted and must continue later through React's resume APIs.

interview.question: What does `prerenderToNodeStream` return?
interview.answer: It is a static server-rendering API from `react-dom/static` that returns a Promise. The resolved `prelude` is a Node.js HTML stream, while `postponed` is serializable state for continuing an incomplete prerender.
interview.followUp: How would you choose between this and `prerender`? Use this function for Node.js Streams; use `prerender` in Web Streams environments such as modern edge runtimes.

interview.question: How does it differ from ordinary streaming SSR?
interview.answer: It waits for data needed by Suspense before the Promise resolves, making it suitable for static site generation. Unlike streaming SSR APIs, it does not progressively emit content as that data arrives.
interview.followUp: Why might it be preferable to `renderToString`? It supports static generation that waits for asynchronous data instead of failing to represent unfinished Suspense content.

interview.question: What should the input tree and bootstrap options contain?
interview.answer: The React node should represent the entire document, so the root application should render `<html>`. Optional `bootstrapScripts` adds script URLs to the generated page, commonly including the script that calls `hydrateRoot`.
interview.followUp: What must happen after delivery to make the page interactive? Load the bootstrap script and hydrate the server-generated markup with `hydrateRoot`.

keyPoints: Use it for static server-side generation when the output must be delivered through a Node.js Stream.
The call is asynchronous and accepts a React node followed by optional rendering options.
The `prelude` value contains the generated HTML and can be piped to a response in chunks.
The `postponed` value can preserve an unfinished prerender for later continuation.
Use `bootstrapScripts` to emit page scripts, including a client entry point used for hydration.
`maxHeadersLength` limits header content supplied to `onHeaders` and defaults to 2000 UTF-16 code units.
Set `namespaceURI` when the root output is SVG or MathML rather than ordinary HTML.
gotchas: Use this API only where Node.js Streams are available; environments with Web Streams should use `prerender` instead.
Pass a root that renders the complete document, including the `<html>` element, rather than only an application fragment.

Profiler.summary: `<Profiler>` measures a React subtree’s rendering performance programmatically. Give it an `id` and an `onRender` callback to receive information about committed updates and their timing.
Profiler.explanation: Wrap a React subtree in Profiler and provide an identifier plus an onRender callback. React invokes the callback after updates commit, supplying timing and render metadata so you can inspect costly subtrees.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: String identifying the UI portion being measured.

parameters.name: onRender
parameters.description: Callback invoked when components within the profiled tree update; it receives render and timing information.

Profiler.returns: A React element that renders its children while reporting profiled commits through onRender.

example.title: Measure a subtree
example.explanation: Wrap the subtree to measure and log each committed render.

useCases.title: Locate expensive subtrees
useCases.scenario: Diagnosing slow updates

useCases.title: Measure separate UI areas
useCases.scenario: Comparing application regions

useCases.title: Collect data with a profiling build
useCases.scenario: Investigating production performance

interview.question: What does Profiler do and when is onRender called?
interview.answer: Profiler measures a React tree programmatically. It requires an id and an onRender callback, which React calls when a component in the profiled tree commits an update.
interview.followUp: How would you isolate performance problems across a large app? Add multiple Profiler boundaries around the areas you want to compare, then inspect each callback’s reported render information.

interview.question: What are Profiler’s required props?
interview.answer: The id is a string naming the UI region being measured. The callback receives information about what rendered and how long it took.
interview.followUp: What trade-off should guide where boundaries are added? Profiling adds CPU and memory overhead, so instrument only the regions needed for diagnosis.

interview.question: Can Profiler collect measurements in a normal production build?
interview.answer: Profiler can be used in production only with a special profiling-enabled production build; ordinary production profiling is disabled by default to avoid overhead.
interview.followUp: What should be compared when investigating a production-only slowdown? Measure the relevant subtree in a profiling build, while remembering that profiling itself changes runtime overhead.

keyPoints: Profiler provides programmatic render-performance measurements for a selected React subtree.
Put the boundary around the components whose rendering behavior you want to analyze.
Use id to label the measured region in callback data and logs.
Supply onRender to receive notifications after updates within the boundary.
Use callback arguments to record rendered content and elapsed render time.
gotchas: Profiling can affect measurements and is off in ordinary production builds; use a profiling-enabled production build when production data is required.
Place separate Profiler boundaries around distinct areas when you need independent measurements.

PropsWithChildren.sourceTitle: Passing Props to a Component – React
PropsWithChildren.summary: Props let parent components send values to child components. They can contain JavaScript values such as objects, arrays, functions, and JSX through children.
PropsWithChildren.explanation: A component receives props from its parent through JSX attributes. Props can contain any JavaScript value, including objects, arrays, and functions. The child reads them from its function parameter, often by destructuring, and can render the special children prop as nested JSX.

parameters.name: props
parameters.description: Information supplied by a parent component through JSX attributes.

parameters.name: children
parameters.description: Nested React content supplied between a component's opening and closing tags.

example.title: Passing an object and a default value
example.explanation: The parent passes an object as the person prop. Avatar receives it by destructuring the props parameter and uses its fields. The size prop has a default value when the parent does not provide one.

useCases.title: Pass component data
useCases.scenario: Send data from a parent to control what a child renders.

useCases.title: Pass structured data
useCases.scenario: Give a reusable component an object with related fields.

useCases.title: Pass children
useCases.scenario: Provide nested JSX to a layout or wrapper component.

useCases.title: Use default values
useCases.scenario: Set a fallback when a prop is omitted.

interview.question: What are props in React?
interview.answer: Props are values a parent gives to a child through JSX. They can be strings, numbers, objects, arrays, functions, or JSX.
interview.followUp: How can a component receive nested JSX? Use the children prop, which contains the JSX placed between the component's opening and closing tags.

interview.question: How does a child component read props?
interview.answer: A function component reads props from its parameter. It can use the full props object or destructure named values, such as function Avatar({ person }).
interview.followUp: How can a component provide a fallback? Destructure a prop with a default value, such as function Avatar({ size = 100 }).

interview.question: What is the children prop?
interview.answer: The children prop contains nested React content. It may be an element, string, number, portal, empty node, or an array of these values.
interview.followUp: How can you count or transform children? React provides Children.count, Children.map, Children.forEach, Children.only, and Children.toArray, but this API can be fragile.

keyPoints: Props look like HTML attributes, but they can carry any JavaScript value.
A parent sends information to a child by placing props on the child JSX tag.
Built-in browser components support documented props that follow browser and HTML behavior.
The special children prop stores nested React content passed between a component's tags.
gotchas: Avoid using the Children API unless you need to transform or inspect the children data structure; prefer clearer component designs when possible.

PropsWithRef.summary: `key` and `ref` are special React props. React uses them internally and does not pass them to components as normal props.
PropsWithRef.explanation: `key` is a special React prop used to identify elements during rendering. React does not pass it to the component as a normal prop, so a component cannot read `props.key`. Pass the value again with another prop when the component needs it for its own logic.

example.title: Pass a key value to a component
example.explanation: React uses `key` to track the element, while the component receives the same value through the separate `id` prop.

useCases.title: Give list items a stable React key
useCases.scenario: Rendering a list

useCases.title: Use a separate prop for component logic
useCases.scenario: Passing an identifier to a child

useCases.title: Treat ref as a React-managed prop
useCases.scenario: Using refs

interview.question: Is `key` available in a component's props?
interview.answer: `key` helps React identify an element, but it is not forwarded to the component. A component that needs the same value must receive it through another prop.
interview.followUp: What should you do when a child needs the identifier used as its key? Pass it explicitly with a separate prop, such as `id`, and read that prop in the child.

interview.question: Which JSX props are special and not forwarded?
interview.answer: Most JSX props are passed to components, but `key` and `ref` are exceptions. React uses both for its own work instead of forwarding them as ordinary props.
interview.followUp: Why keep the React hint separate from application data? It separates React's rendering behavior from the values the component uses for its own logic.

interview.question: How can a component receive the value used as its key?
interview.answer: Use `key={result.id}` when React needs to identify the element, and use `id={result.id}` when the component also needs that identifier. The two props serve different purposes.
interview.followUp: Can the child infer the key from `props`? No. The child must receive the value through a normal prop if it needs access to it.

keyPoints: React treats `key` and `ref` differently from ordinary JSX props.
Normal JSX props are forwarded to the receiving component.
Pass a second, ordinary prop when the child needs the value used for `key`.
gotchas: Do not try to read `key` inside the receiving component. It is handled by React and is not forwarded as a normal prop.

PureComponent.summary: PureComponent is a class base that can skip re-renders when props and state are shallowly unchanged. React recommends function components for new code.
PureComponent.explanation: PureComponent is a class base that uses shallow comparisons of props and state to skip some re-renders. Use it mainly when keeping an existing class component; React recommends function components for new code.
PureComponent.syntax: class MyComponent extends PureComponent { render() { return ...; } }

example.title: Skip unchanged props in a class component
example.explanation: Greeting can skip a render when the parent changes only address, because its name prop stays the same.

useCases.title: Optimize an existing class component
useCases.scenario: You maintain a class component and want to avoid renders caused by unchanged props and state.

useCases.title: Skip unrelated parent updates
useCases.scenario: A parent updates for one reason, but a class child receives unchanged top-level props.

useCases.title: Migrate to memo
useCases.scenario: You are replacing a PureComponent class with a function component.

interview.question: What does PureComponent do?
interview.answer: PureComponent is a subclass of Component. It adds shallow comparisons for props and state, so React can skip a render when those values are unchanged.
interview.followUp: What does shallow comparison imply? It checks top-level values, so changing an object or array reference can count as a change even when its contents look similar.

interview.question: When can PureComponent skip work?
interview.answer: A parent render normally causes its child to render. A PureComponent can skip that child render when its new props and state pass the shallow equality check.
interview.followUp: What can still trigger a render? A change to context used by the component can still re-render it.

interview.question: How do you migrate from PureComponent?
interview.answer: For new code, use a function component instead. To preserve the comparable prop optimization during migration, wrap the function in memo.
interview.followUp: Does memo replace every PureComponent behavior? No. memo compares props, while function state updates have their own same-value bailout.

keyPoints: It keeps the APIs available to class components that already extend Component.
Its built-in update check is shallow, not a deep comparison of nested data.
A parent update can otherwise cause the child class component to render again.
The optimization applies when both the incoming props and state remain shallowly equal.
The render method should produce the same result when props, state, and context have not changed.
gotchas: Prefer function components for new code. PureComponent is mainly useful when maintaining an existing class component.
When replacing PureComponent with a function, memo compares props, but not state. State updates already avoid a render when the state value is unchanged.

React Compiler.summary: React Compiler is a build-time tool that automatically adds memoization to React components and hooks. It can reduce unnecessary re-renders and repeated expensive calculations, so new code often needs less manual useMemo, useCallback, or React.memo.
React Compiler.explanation: React Compiler analyzes React components and hooks during the build. It follows the Rules of React and adds memoization automatically, which can skip unnecessary component updates and repeated calculations without requiring manual memoization in new code.

example.title: Install and configure React Compiler
example.explanation: Install the compiler as a development dependency and place its Babel plugin before other plugins.

useCases.title: Skip unnecessary child re-renders
useCases.scenario: A parent updates while some child inputs are unchanged.

useCases.title: Reuse expensive render calculations
useCases.scenario: A component processes a large data set during rendering.

useCases.title: Adopt optimization incrementally
useCases.scenario: An existing application needs gradual adoption.

interview.question: What problem does React Compiler solve?
interview.answer: React Compiler is a build-time tool. It understands the Rules of React and adds memoization to components and hooks, so React can skip unnecessary updates and some expensive calculations.
interview.followUp: What does it optimize? It mainly skips cascading component re-renders and repeated expensive calculations used by components or hooks.

interview.question: Which React versions and build tools can use it?
interview.answer: React Compiler supports React 19 best and also supports React 17 and 18. It can be integrated with Babel, Vite, Metro, and other supported build tools.
interview.followUp: What must happen in a Babel setup? The compiler must run first, before other transformations, so it receives the original source.

interview.question: Should existing manual memoization be removed?
interview.answer: New code can usually rely on the compiler for memoization. Existing useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo calls should normally remain unless they are removed and carefully tested, because removal can change compiled output.
interview.followUp: How can optimization be checked? React DevTools shows a “Memo ✨” badge for optimized components.

keyPoints: Optimization happens during the build, before the application runs.
The compiler can prevent unchanged parts of a component tree from rendering again after an update.
It can cache costly calculations made inside components or hooks when their relevant inputs stay unchanged.
Standalone functions do not receive compiler memoization automatically.
Using the compiler is optional, although future React features may depend on it.
The badge in React DevTools is one way to verify that compilation is active.
gotchas: In Babel, put the compiler plugin before every other Babel plugin so it can analyze the original source.
An ESLint compiler violation only prevents optimization for the affected component or hook; other code can still be compiled.
Manual memoization can fail when JSX creates a new callback during every render.
For a costly shared function, consider separate memoization after profiling because compiler caching is limited to React components and hooks.

ReactElement.summary: createElement creates a React element without JSX. Give it a valid type, props or null, and optional children.
ReactElement.explanation: Call createElement with a valid component type, a props object or null, and zero or more children. React returns an element whose props come from the supplied props; key and ref are special and are not read as ordinary element props.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: A valid React component type, such as a tag name string or a React component.

parameters.name: props
parameters.description: An object of props, or null. Null is treated like an empty object.

parameters.name: ...children
parameters.description: Zero or more child values for the element.

example.title: Create and check an element
example.explanation: This creates a button element without JSX and checks that the result is a React element.

useCases.title: Create elements directly
useCases.scenario: A project does not use JSX.

useCases.title: Use a dynamic type
useCases.scenario: Code needs to build an element from a tag or component value.

useCases.title: Check an element
useCases.scenario: Code needs to verify the result before using it.

interview.question: What does createElement do?
interview.answer: createElement creates a React element without JSX. Its arguments are a component type, props or null, and any number of children.
interview.followUp: What can type contain? It can be a tag name such as 'div' or 'span', a function or class component, or a special component such as Fragment.

interview.question: What values are valid for type and props?
interview.answer: The type must be a valid React component type. It may be a string tag name or a React component, including a function, class, or special component.
interview.followUp: What happens if props is null? React treats null like an empty props object.

interview.question: How can you check whether a value is a React element?
interview.answer: createElement returns a React element. isValidElement can check that result, while numbers and strings are React nodes but are not React elements.
interview.followUp: Which values does isValidElement accept? JSX elements and objects returned by createElement are accepted; arbitrary objects, numbers, and strings are not.

keyPoints: Use createElement when you need to build a React element without JSX.
The function receives the element type, its props, and its children.
The type must be a valid tag name or React component type.
Pass an object for props, or pass null when there are no props.
The returned element contains the props supplied to createElement.
JSX elements and createElement results are React elements.
gotchas: Do not treat key or ref like normal props. React handles them specially.

ReactNode.sourceTitle: prerenderToNodeStream – React API Reference Static APIs
ReactNode.summary: `prerenderToNodeStream` renders a complete React document as static HTML in a Node.js stream. Await the result, then pipe its `prelude` stream to the response.
ReactNode.explanation: Call this API with the React tree for the full document. It waits for the app's data before returning a static Node.js stream. Pipe the returned `prelude` to the response. Use `hydrateRoot` in the browser if the page should become interactive.
ReactNode.syntax: const { prelude, postponed } = await prerenderToNodeStream(reactNode, options?);

parameters.name: reactNode
parameters.description: The React node to render as static HTML. It should represent the entire document.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional static generation settings, including bootstrap scripts, modules, inline script content, and an ID prefix.

ReactNode.returns: A promise that resolves to an object containing `prelude`, a static HTML Node.js stream, and possibly `postponed`.

example.title: Prerender an app
example.explanation: This creates static HTML, adds a client script, and pipes the result to a Node.js response.

useCases.title: Generate static server HTML
useCases.scenario: A Node.js route must return HTML after the app's data is ready.

useCases.title: Create HTML for hydration
useCases.scenario: A page needs HTML for a client that will run React afterward.

useCases.title: Add startup scripts
useCases.scenario: A page should include client entry scripts as part of the output.

interview.question: What does `prerenderToNodeStream` return?
interview.answer: It renders a React tree as static HTML and returns a promise with a `prelude` stream. The server can pipe that stream to a Node.js response.
interview.followUp: How would you make the result interactive? Include a bootstrap script that calls `hydrateRoot` on the client.

interview.question: What should the React tree contain?
interview.answer: The React node should represent the complete document. Its component should render the `<html>` tag, not only an application fragment.
interview.followUp: What should be passed when rendering only part of a page? This API is documented for the full document, so use another rendering approach for that case.

interview.question: How do the bootstrap options differ?
interview.answer: `bootstrapScripts` adds script URLs for client code, while `bootstrapModules` adds module scripts. `bootstrapScriptContent` adds an inline script.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid client-side React? Leave these bootstrap options out.

keyPoints: Use the function when you need static HTML from a React tree.
The first argument is the React node to render.
`bootstrapScripts` accepts script URL strings for client startup code.
Use `bootstrapModules` when the client entry uses JavaScript modules.
`identifierPrefix` helps prevent `useId` collisions between multiple roots.
gotchas: Use this API only with Node.js streams. For Web Streams, use `prerender` instead.
Pass a tree that represents the whole document, including the `<html>` element.
Do not add bootstrap scripts when the generated page should stay static.

ReactPortal.summary: createPortal renders React children into a different part of the DOM while preserving their place in the React tree. It is commonly used for UI such as modals that must escape container boundaries.
ReactPortal.explanation: createPortal returns a React node that places renderable children inside an existing DOM node. The portal changes where those nodes appear physically, but the content remains a child of the component that created it for React behavior such as context and event propagation.

parameters.name: children
parameters.description: Any React-renderable content, such as JSX, a fragment, string, number, or an array of these.

parameters.name: domNode
parameters.description: An already-existing DOM node that receives the rendered children.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: An optional key for the portal.

ReactPortal.returns: A React node that can be rendered in JSX or returned from a React component; React places its children inside the supplied DOM node.

example.title: Render a modal through a portal
example.explanation: This component places the dialog under document.body while keeping it in the React tree.

useCases.title: Modals and dialogs
useCases.scenario: A dialog needs to escape an ancestor's clipping or stacking context.

useCases.title: Toasts and alerts
useCases.scenario: A transient notification should mount in a document-level host.

useCases.title: Overlays and floating UI
useCases.scenario: A menu or tooltip must render outside an overflow-constrained container.

interview.question: What is a portal and how do you create one?
interview.answer: Use createPortal from react-dom with renderable children and an existing DOM node. React inserts the children into that node while the portal remains part of the originating component's React tree.
interview.followUp: What changes when the target element changes? React recreates the portal content when a different DOM node is supplied during an update.

interview.question: What does a portal change, and what does it preserve?
interview.answer: A portal changes only the physical DOM placement. The JSX still behaves as a child of the component that renders it, so React relationships are preserved.
interview.followUp: Why are portals useful for dialogs? They let dialog markup escape clipping or stacking containers while remaining owned by the dialog component.

interview.question: What arguments does createPortal accept?
interview.answer: The children argument accepts anything React can render, including JSX, fragments, strings, numbers, or arrays of these. The domNode argument identifies the already-existing destination node.
interview.followUp: What should be checked before rendering into a destination? Ensure the destination exists before the portal is rendered and avoid changing it unnecessarily.

keyPoints: Use it when a component's rendered DOM must live outside its usual container.
Portalization affects physical placement rather than the component's React ownership.
The originating component remains the React parent of portal content.
Treat the result as renderable output, either embedded in JSX or returned directly.
The children input supports ordinary React-renderable values, not only element objects.
gotchas: Pass an existing DOM node; a target that has not been created cannot receive portal content.
Keep the target node stable across updates unless recreating the portal subtree is intentional.

Reducer.summary: Reducer is the function passed to useReducer to define how actions transform current state into next state. React calls it during dispatch and uses its return value for the next render.
Reducer.explanation: Reducer is the function shape used by useReducer: it accepts the current state and an action, and returns the next state. React invokes it after dispatch, stores the returned state, re-renders the component, and updates the UI.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: The current state value supplied to the reducer.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: The dispatched action describing the requested update.

Reducer.returns: The next state, with the same State type as the reducer's state input.

example.title: Typed reducer with useReducer
example.explanation: This reducer receives the current state and an action, then returns the next state used by useReducer.

useCases.title: Centralize complex state updates
useCases.scenario: A component has several related state transitions, such as adding, editing, and removing items.

useCases.title: Represent updates as actions
useCases.scenario: Event handlers should describe user intent without duplicating transition logic.

useCases.title: Type state transitions
useCases.scenario: A reducer's state and action shapes need compile-time guarantees.

interview.question: What is a reducer in React?
interview.answer: A reducer is a function that receives the current state and an action, then returns the next state. In React, useReducer passes the current state and dispatched action to it, stores the result, and re-renders the component.
interview.followUp: What makes a reducer suitable for React state updates? It must be pure, deterministic for the same inputs, and must return the complete next state rather than mutating the existing one.

interview.question: How does dispatch interact with a reducer?
interview.answer: useReducer returns exactly two values: the current state and a dispatch function. Dispatching an action causes React to calculate the next state through the reducer and trigger a re-render.
interview.followUp: Why use a reducer instead of several setters? A reducer centralizes update rules, which is useful when state transitions are related or there are multiple action types.

interview.question: What types can a reducer's state and action have?
interview.answer: The reducer and action types are application-defined; React does not restrict their types. The reducer still needs to accept state and action arguments and return the next state.
interview.followUp: How is initial state handled? useReducer uses initialArg directly unless an optional init function is supplied, in which case it uses init(initialArg).

keyPoints: A reducer contains the rules for transforming state in response to dispatched actions.
React invokes the reducer with the latest state and the action supplied to dispatch.
The reducer's output becomes the component's next state.
After reduction, React stores the result, renders with it, and refreshes the visible interface.
gotchas: Keep reducers pure: do not perform side effects, mutate the existing state, or return an unrelated result.
The hook that consumes a reducer must be called at the top level, never inside loops or conditions.

Ref.summary: useRef stores a value in a stable object without causing re-renders when the value changes. It is useful for non-visual data, such as timer IDs, and for accessing DOM nodes.
Ref.explanation: useRef creates a stable object with a mutable current property. React keeps the same object between renders, but changing current does not render the component again. Use refs for values that do not affect the displayed result, or for DOM nodes used by event handlers and effects.

parameters.name: initialValue
parameters.description: The starting value for current. React uses this value only during the initial render.

Ref.returns: An object with one mutable property, current. React returns the same object on later renders.

example.title: Focus an input with a ref
example.explanation: This ref starts as null. React assigns the input element to current after mounting, so the click handler can focus it.

useCases.title: Store timer IDs
useCases.scenario: Keep an interval or timeout ID between renders so an event handler can stop it later.

useCases.title: Access a DOM node
useCases.scenario: Focus, scroll, measure, or otherwise use a browser DOM API on a rendered node.

useCases.title: Lazy initialization
useCases.scenario: Keep an object that is expensive to create, initializing it once when current is null.

useCases.title: Track list nodes
useCases.scenario: Maintain DOM nodes for a dynamic list with a ref callback and a Map.

interview.question: How does useRef differ from useState?
interview.answer: useRef returns an object with one current property. React keeps that object between renders, and changing current does not cause another render.
interview.followUp: When should state be used instead? Use state when the value affects the JSX or other visual output, because state updates schedule a render.

interview.question: How do you use useRef to access a DOM element?
interview.answer: Create a ref with useRef(null), pass it to a DOM element with the ref JSX attribute, and read current from an event handler or effect. React fills current with the DOM node after the commit and sets it back to null when the node is removed.
interview.followUp: Why can current be null? It is null before the first DOM commit and after the referenced node is removed.

interview.question: What is a practical use for a value ref?
interview.answer: A ref is useful for information that persists but does not affect rendering, such as a timer ID. Store the returned ID in ref.current and read it later to cancel the timer.
interview.followUp: Why not use a normal variable? A normal variable is recreated on each render, while the ref object persists for that component instance.

keyPoints: The hook returns an object whose only property is current. It begins with the value passed to useRef.
React returns the same ref object on later renders, so its stored value survives rendering.
You can assign a new value to current directly. This value can be a number, object, function, or DOM node.
Each mounted component instance has its own ref data. Refs are not shared through variables outside the component.
When a ref is passed to a DOM node, React places that node in current after the DOM is committed.
gotchas: Do not read or change ref.current while rendering, except for predictable one-time initialization. Use an event handler or an effect instead.
A ref cannot update text shown by the component. Use state when a changed value must appear in the UI.
A ref on a custom component does not automatically point to its inner DOM node. The component must accept and pass the ref, or expose a limited handle.

RefCallback.summary: RefCallback is the function form of a React ref. React calls it with the attached DOM node and, in React 19, can run a cleanup function returned by the callback when the node detaches.
RefCallback.explanation: RefCallback is the callback form of a React ref. React invokes it with the referenced value when attaching, and in React 19 a returned cleanup function runs when the ref detaches; if no cleanup is returned, React uses null for detachment.

parameters.name: node
parameters.description: The referenced DOM node supplied when the callback ref attaches; the page documents this as a DOM node.

RefCallback.returns: An optional cleanup function. React calls it when the ref is detached; if omitted, React calls the callback with null on detachment.

example.title: Callback ref with cleanup
example.explanation: The callback receives the input element when React attaches the ref and returns cleanup that runs when React detaches it.

useCases.title: External DOM integration
useCases.scenario: Register or unregister a DOM node with an external system when it appears or disappears.

useCases.title: Imperative node setup
useCases.scenario: Measure, focus, observe, or otherwise act on a node immediately after attachment.

useCases.title: Dynamic lists
useCases.scenario: Track a dynamic collection of nodes where each item needs attachment-specific registration.

interview.question: What is a callback ref, and what does it receive?
interview.answer: A callback ref is a function passed to ref instead of a ref object. React calls it with the DOM node when attached; in React 19, the callback can return cleanup that runs when detached.
interview.followUp: What happens without returned cleanup? React calls the callback with null on detachment, so code must handle that value or use the React 19 cleanup form.

interview.question: Why can an inline callback ref run during rerenders?
interview.answer: React compares callback identity. If a different callback is supplied, React cleans up the old ref and attaches the new one; an inline function can therefore cause repeated setup during rerenders.
interview.followUp: How can repeated work be avoided? Reuse the callback function reference, for example by defining it stably or memoizing it when appropriate.

interview.question: Why is cleanup especially important with Strict Mode?
interview.answer: Callback refs need symmetric cleanup because setup may run more than once in development Strict Mode. Returning cleanup that reverses subscriptions, registrations, or other effects prevents leaks and exposes bugs early.
interview.followUp: What kind of bug does missing cleanup cause? External registrations can accumulate across setup cycles, producing stale references, memory leaks, or duplicated behavior.

keyPoints: A callback ref is an alternative to passing a ref object and is useful when attachment itself should trigger imperative work.
React supplies the attached DOM node to the callback when the element enters the screen.
React 19 runs the returned cleanup when the referenced node is removed.
Changing the callback identity causes React to process the ref again, which can repeat setup and cleanup.
Without a returned cleanup function, detachment is signaled by calling the callback with null.
Treat callback refs as setup-and-cleanup lifecycles, especially when they interact with systems outside React.
gotchas: Strict Mode deliberately exercises callback-ref setup and cleanup an extra time in development, so cleanup must fully undo setup.

RefObject.summary: useRef remembers a value without causing a re-render when that value changes. It can also hold a DOM node for imperative actions.
RefObject.explanation: useRef creates a stable object with a mutable current property. React does not re-render the component when current changes, so refs are useful for values or DOM nodes that rendering does not need.

parameters.name: initialValue
parameters.description: The value used for the ref object's initial current property. It may have any type, and later renders ignore this argument.

RefObject.returns: An object with a mutable current property. React keeps the same object across renders.

example.title: Focus a DOM element with a ref
example.explanation: The ref stores the input DOM node after React renders it. The button reads current and calls focus without causing a re-render.

useCases.title: Store non-visual component data
useCases.scenario: Keep an interval ID, timeout ID, or other mutable value between renders without displaying it.

useCases.title: Access a DOM node
useCases.scenario: Read or control a browser element, such as focusing an input.

useCases.title: Retain a value between renders
useCases.scenario: Keep a stable object available to event handlers across renders.

interview.question: What does useRef return?
interview.answer: useRef returns an object whose current property starts with the supplied initial value. React returns the same object on later renders.
interview.followUp: When should state be used instead? Use state when a value must trigger a re-render and update the displayed result.

interview.question: How do you use a ref to access a DOM element?
interview.answer: A ref can hold a DOM node when passed to a JSX element through its ref attribute. After React attaches the node, code can read that node from current.
interview.followUp: How can a component use the node safely? Check that current is not null before calling a DOM method, because the node may not be attached yet.

interview.question: How are refs different from state?
interview.answer: Changing current does not trigger rendering. This makes refs suitable for values needed by event handlers or imperative DOM actions but not for displayed data.
interview.followUp: What should replace a ref for displayed data? Use state so React knows it must render again when the value changes.

keyPoints: Use useRef for information that the component must remember but does not need to display.
The returned ref object has one main property, current.
The first argument sets current during the initial render.
The ref object stays stable across renders.
Passing a ref to JSX lets React place the related DOM node in current.
gotchas: The current value is mutable, so code can replace it after the ref is created.
Do not call useRef inside conditions, loops, or nested functions.

render.summary: Deprecated legacy API that mounts a React node into a browser DOM element. React 19+ code should use createRoot from react-dom/client instead.
render.explanation: The legacy render function places a React node into a browser DOM element and optionally invokes a callback after placement. It was replaced by createRoot in React 18, so React 19+ applications should create a root and call its render method instead.

parameters.name: reactNode
parameters.description: The React node to display, commonly JSX but also an element, string, number, null, or undefined.

parameters.name: domNode
parameters.description: The browser DOM element whose contents React will manage.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Optional function invoked after the component is placed into the DOM.

render.returns: Usually null; for a class component, an instance of that component may be returned.

example.title: React 19+ replacement
example.explanation: Use the supported React 19+ root API instead of the deprecated render function.

useCases.title: Legacy migration
useCases.scenario: Maintaining an older React application that still imports render from react-dom.

useCases.title: Codebase maintenance
useCases.scenario: Understanding an existing entry point before replacing its mounting logic.

interview.question: What does the legacy render function do?
interview.answer: The function accepts a React node, a browser DOM element, and an optional callback. React takes ownership of the DOM inside the supplied element and updates it as the React tree changes.
interview.followUp: What should replace it in React 19? Use createRoot from react-dom/client, then call the root object's render method with the application component.

interview.question: What are the main arguments?
interview.answer: The React node is the content to display, such as JSX, an element made with createElement, text, a number, null, or undefined. The DOM element is the container whose contents React manages.
interview.followUp: Can the container be any value? No; it must be a DOM element suitable for browser rendering.

interview.question: What does render return?
interview.answer: The function generally returns null. A legacy class-component case can instead produce an instance of that component, but this should not be used as a reason to retain the deprecated API.
interview.followUp: How should modern code access an application root? Keep the root returned by createRoot and use its render method; do not depend on the old function's return behavior.

keyPoints: Its purpose is to mount a React node into a browser DOM container.
The function starts displaying the supplied component tree in the chosen element.
The first argument is commonly JSX, although other React-node values are accepted.
The second argument determines where the supplied React content appears.
After mounting, React controls updates within that container.
The optional callback runs after the component has been inserted.
For React 19+ applications, use createRoot rather than this deprecated function.
gotchas: Do not use this API for new React 19+ code; createRoot is the supported replacement.
Existing usage is transitional and may stop working after a future major release.
Do not expect a root handle from the function.
The return value is an unusual legacy exception for class components, not a general-purpose application API.

renderToPipeableStream.summary: Renders a React tree as HTML into a pipeable Node.js Stream. Use onShellReady for progressive streaming or onAllReady when the complete output must be ready first.
renderToPipeableStream.explanation: Call renderToPipeableStream with the complete React document and optional callbacks, then pipe the returned output into a Writable Node.js stream. Start in onShellReady for progressive streaming, use onAllReady for crawlers or static generation, and abort when rendering should stop.

parameters.name: reactNode
parameters.description: The React node to render as HTML; it should represent the entire document.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional configuration object containing callbacks, bootstrap scripts, namespace settings, and other rendering options.

renderToPipeableStream.returns: An object containing pipe, which writes HTML to a Writable Node.js Stream, and abort, which stops server rendering and allows the remaining UI to render on the client.

example.title: Stream a complete document from Node.js
example.explanation: Creates a Node.js streaming response, starts piping when the shell is ready, and aborts rendering if the request closes.

useCases.title: Progressive server streaming
useCases.scenario: Send the initial document structure quickly while Suspense-delayed sections continue arriving.

useCases.title: Crawler and static generation output
useCases.scenario: Produce a complete HTML response before handing it to a crawler or static-generation pipeline.

useCases.title: Request cancellation
useCases.scenario: Stop work when the client disconnects and let the browser finish the remaining UI.

interview.question: What does renderToPipeableStream return?
interview.answer: It renders a React tree as HTML into a pipeable Node.js Stream. The returned pipe method writes to a Writable Node.js Stream, while abort stops server rendering and lets the rest render on the client.
interview.followUp: When should streaming begin? Start in onShellReady for normal progressive responses; use onAllReady when the consumer needs the complete output, such as a crawler.

interview.question: What are the function's inputs?
interview.answer: The first argument is the React node representing the document to render. The optional options object configures bootstrap scripts, callbacks, namespaces, and other server-rendering behavior.
interview.followUp: What must the root node contain? It should represent the entire document, including the root html element.

interview.question: Which environments should use this function?
interview.answer: This API targets Node.js Streams. For Deno and modern edge runtimes that use Web Streams, the corresponding API is renderToReadableStream.
interview.followUp: Why not use renderToString for progressive loading? It returns a string immediately and does not stream content as it becomes available.

keyPoints: Use it for server-rendering React HTML directly into a Node.js stream.
Destructure pipe and abort from the returned result.
The shell callback indicates that the initial page structure is ready to send.
Use onAllReady when output should wait until every rendered boundary is ready.
Provide client script paths when the streamed document needs browser-side startup code.
The namespace option defaults to HTML and can be changed for SVG or MathML roots.
gotchas: Use renderToReadableStream instead in environments that provide Web Streams rather than Node.js Streams.
Render the complete document from the root component, not only the application content.
Choosing the wrong callback changes whether incomplete Suspense content can stream progressively.

renderToReadableStream.summary: Renders a complete React tree as HTML into a Web ReadableStream, intended for streaming server rendering in Web Streams environments. The returned promise resolves when the shell is ready.
renderToReadableStream.explanation: The function asynchronously renders a React tree as HTML for Web Streams environments. Once the shell is ready, its promise resolves with a ReadableStream that can be placed in a Response; the stream also exposes allReady for waiting until every Suspense-dependent part has finished.

parameters.name: reactNode
parameters.description: The React node to render as HTML; it should represent the entire document, including the html element.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional object containing streaming options such as bootstrapScripts, signal, namespaceURI, and progressiveChunkSize.

renderToReadableStream.returns: A Promise resolving to a Readable Web Stream when the shell renders successfully; the promise rejects if shell rendering fails. The stream has an allReady Promise for completion of all content.

example.title: Stream a server-rendered document
example.explanation: Renders the complete document into a Web ReadableStream and returns it as an HTTP response.

useCases.title: Stream SSR HTML from a request handler
useCases.scenario: Edge or Web Streams server rendering

useCases.title: Reveal async content progressively
useCases.scenario: Suspense-based server rendering

useCases.title: Wait for allReady to send complete HTML
useCases.scenario: Crawlers and static generation

useCases.title: Pair bootstrap scripts with hydrateRoot
useCases.scenario: Client hydration

interview.question: What does renderToReadableStream return?
interview.answer: It returns a Promise because the shell may need asynchronous rendering before a stream can be provided. A successful shell resolves to a Readable Web Stream; a shell failure rejects the promise.
interview.followUp: How would you serve crawlers? Await the returned stream’s allReady promise before returning the response, which sends final HTML instead of progressively revealed content.

interview.question: How is it used in an edge-style request handler?
interview.answer: Pass the complete React document as reactNode and optionally provide an options object containing streaming configuration. The root component should produce the html element and the result can be used as the body of a Response.
interview.followUp: How do you make the generated document interactive? Supply bootstrap scripts and hydrate the server HTML on the client with hydrateRoot.

interview.question: When should you choose this API over renderToPipeableStream?
interview.answer: The API is intended for runtimes implementing Web Streams, such as modern edge environments. For Node.js, the documentation directs you to renderToPipeableStream instead.
interview.followUp: What trade-off does allReady introduce? It allows complete output suitable for crawlers or static generation, but removes progressive loading.

keyPoints: Use it for streaming server-rendered React HTML through the Web Streams API.
The output is HTML streamed from the server rather than a single eagerly assembled string.
The initial shell controls when the function becomes usable for constructing the response.
After waiting for allReady, the stream represents the completed document without progressive delivery.
Client hydration is the step that turns the streamed server markup into an interactive React application.
gotchas: This API relies on Web Streams, so Node.js applications should use the Node-oriented streaming API instead.
Awaiting allReady before sending the response produces complete HTML but disables progressive streaming.

renderToStaticMarkup.summary: renderToStaticMarkup converts a React tree into a non-interactive HTML string. Use it on the server when you need static markup rather than hydrated or streamed output.
renderToStaticMarkup.explanation: React walks the given node and returns the resulting markup as a string. The output is intended for non-interactive HTML, such as content sent in an HTTP response. It does not include the setup needed to hydrate the tree on the client.

parameters.name: reactNode
parameters.description: The React node to convert into HTML, such as a JSX element.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional server-rendering settings. It may include identifierPrefix, a string prefix for IDs generated by useId.

example.title: Render a static React tree
example.explanation: This creates an HTML string from a React component. A server can send that string in its response.

useCases.title: Send static HTML from a server
useCases.scenario: A server route needs to return initial, non-interactive page markup as text.

useCases.title: Avoid generated ID conflicts
useCases.scenario: A page contains more than one React root and generated useId values need distinct prefixes.

useCases.title: Render without streaming
useCases.scenario: The runtime does not provide a suitable stream API and a complete string is needed.

interview.question: What does renderToStaticMarkup do?
interview.answer: It renders a React node into an HTML string. The result is non-interactive and can be sent as part of a server response.
interview.followUp: Can the result be hydrated later? No. The documentation says output from this API cannot be hydrated.

interview.question: What arguments does it accept?
interview.answer: The first argument is the React node to render, such as a JSX element. The optional options object can include identifierPrefix.
interview.followUp: Why use identifierPrefix? It helps prevent ID conflicts when multiple React roots use useId on one page.

interview.question: When should this API be used instead of a streaming API?
interview.answer: Use it when a non-interactive HTML string is needed in an environment without streaming support. Streaming APIs provide more functionality when the environment supports streams.
interview.followUp: What should be used in a Node.js streaming environment? Use the Node.js stream API renderToPipeableStream instead.

keyPoints: The function converts a React tree into HTML text without client-side interaction support.
It is designed for top-level server rendering, often before sending the initial response.
The required input can be any React node, including JSX such as a component element.
Set identifierPrefix when several roots share a page and their generated IDs must not collide.
The return value is markup represented as a JavaScript string.
This non-streaming API has fewer capabilities than React's server rendering APIs that use streams.
gotchas: Do not use this output with hydration APIs. The resulting page is not connected to React on the client.
Suspense support is limited. If rendering suspends, the fallback is returned immediately.
Although it can run in a browser, prefer rendering into a DOM node for client-side HTML.

renderToString.summary: renderToString converts a React tree into an HTML string on the server. Send the string in the response, then use hydrateRoot in the browser to make the matching HTML interactive.
renderToString.explanation: The function synchronously turns a React node into an HTML string. A server can send that string as the initial response, and the browser can use hydrateRoot with the same tree to add interactivity.

parameters.name: reactNode
parameters.description: The React node to convert to HTML, such as <App />.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional server-rendering settings. The documented option is identifierPrefix, a prefix for useId-generated IDs.

example.title: Render and hydrate an app
example.explanation: Render the app on the server, send the returned HTML, and hydrate matching markup in the browser.

useCases.title: Server-rendered HTML
useCases.scenario: A server needs a simple, non-streaming initial HTML response.

useCases.title: Avoid generated ID conflicts
useCases.scenario: Several React roots use useId on one page.

useCases.title: Non-streaming environments
useCases.scenario: A server environment does not provide stream support.

interview.question: What does renderToString return?
interview.answer: It accepts a React node and optional server-rendering options, then returns an HTML string. The server can include that string in its response.
interview.followUp: What should replace it for streamed Node.js output? Use renderToPipeableStream, which is the Node.js streaming alternative.

interview.question: How does renderToString handle Suspense?
interview.answer: It has limited Suspense support. If rendering suspends, it immediately outputs the closest Suspense boundary's fallback instead of waiting for the content.
interview.followUp: How can static generation include suspended data? Use prerender, which waits for data before resolving.

interview.question: Why might identifierPrefix be needed?
interview.answer: The identifierPrefix option adds a prefix to IDs created by useId. When hydrating, use the same prefix with hydrateRoot so IDs do not conflict across roots.
interview.followUp: When is a different rendering API better? Choose renderToPipeableStream or renderToReadableStream for streaming, and prerender for data-dependent static HTML.

keyPoints: Call it at the top level of server application rendering, not inside ordinary components.
Hydration is a separate client step after the server sends the generated markup.
Set identifierPrefix when several roots share a page and their generated IDs could collide.
Keep the server and client identifierPrefix values identical during hydration.
gotchas: It does not wait for suspended content. It puts the nearest Suspense fallback into the returned HTML.
Use a streaming API when content should arrive while it loads, or use a static prerender API when generation must wait for data.
Do not use this server API in browser code just to turn a component into HTML.

resume.sourceTitle: resume – React API Reference Server APIs
resume.summary: `resume` continues a pre-rendered React tree and streams its HTML through a Readable Web Stream. It uses the postponed state produced by `prerender`.
resume.explanation: `resume` continues a React tree after `prerender` stopped and returned postponed state. It produces HTML in a Readable Web Stream, which can be piped to a Writable Web Stream. React starts again at the root and skips only parts that were fully pre-rendered.
resume.syntax: const stream = await resume(reactNode, postponedState, options?)

parameters.name: reactNode
parameters.description: The React node passed to `prerender`, usually the complete application document.

parameters.name: postponedState
parameters.description: The opaque state returned by a `prerender` API and loaded from storage.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional streaming settings, such as `nonce`, `signal`, `onBrowserBailout`, and `onError`.

resume.returns: A promise for a Readable Web Stream. The stream can be piped to a Writable Web Stream and has an `allReady` promise.

example.title: Resume a pre-rendered tree
example.explanation: Resume the saved render and send its HTML to a writable Web Stream.

useCases.title: Resume server rendering
useCases.scenario: Continue a page render after saving postponed work, then pipe the result to a web response.

useCases.title: Produce complete HTML
useCases.scenario: Wait for `stream.allReady` before sending complete HTML to a crawler or static generator.

interview.question: What does `resume` do?
interview.answer: It continues rendering a tree that was previously started with `prerender`. It accepts the same React node and the saved postponed state, then returns a promise for a Readable Web Stream.
interview.followUp: What happens if a component was fully pre-rendered? React skips that component and its finished children; incomplete work is rendered again from the root.

interview.question: How can you wait for the complete result?
interview.answer: The returned stream has an `allReady` promise. Waiting for it ensures that all rendering is complete before the response is returned, which is useful for crawlers or static output.
interview.followUp: What trade-off does this create? It prevents progressive loading because the final HTML is held until rendering finishes.

interview.question: Which environments is `resume` intended for?
interview.answer: `resume` uses Web Streams. A Node.js application should use the corresponding Node.js stream API instead of this function.
interview.followUp: Why must the application choose the matching API? The stream types differ, so the result must be consumed by the kind of writable stream supported by the runtime.

keyPoints: Call `resume` with the original React node and postponed state to continue HTML rendering.
The postponed state is opaque. Load the value saved after a `prerender` call.
The React node should represent the whole document, including the `<html>` element.
The returned stream exposes `allReady`, a promise that settles after all rendering finishes.
Resume walks from the root and continues at the first part that was not completely pre-rendered.
gotchas: Use this API with Web Streams. For Node.js, use the Node.js stream API instead.
Pass bootstrap script options to the `prerender` call, not to `resume`.
Do not set `identifierPrefix` only during resume. It must match the value used by `prerender`.
Waiting for `allReady` removes progressive loading, so use it only when complete HTML is needed.

resumeAndPrerender.sourceTitle: resumeAndPrerender – React API Reference Static APIs
resumeAndPrerender.summary: resumeAndPrerender continues a paused React prerender and returns static HTML as a Web Stream. Use it for static site generation when a previous prerender produced postponed state.
resumeAndPrerender.explanation: resumeAndPrerender continues a previously stopped React prerender and returns static HTML as a Web Stream. It is useful for static site generation when rendering was split into multiple stages.

parameters.name: reactNode
parameters.description: The React node used by the earlier prerender or by an earlier resumeAndPrerender call. It should represent the whole document.

parameters.name: postponedState
parameters.description: The opaque postponed object returned by a prerender API and loaded from storage.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional streaming settings, such as bootstrapScripts, signal, and onBrowserBailout.

resumeAndPrerender.returns: A Promise resolving to an object with prelude, a Web Stream containing HTML, and postponed, an opaque serializable state that can be passed to resume or resumeAndPrerender if rendering is interrupted.

example.title: Continue a postponed render
example.explanation: Load the saved state, continue rendering the same tree, and send the returned HTML stream. The client should hydrate the document with hydrateRoot.

useCases.title: Continue partial prerendering
useCases.scenario: A prerender was stopped before all Suspense content was ready.

useCases.title: Generate static pages
useCases.scenario: A build or server process needs complete HTML after loading all data.

useCases.title: Send an HTML stream
useCases.scenario: The application uses Web Streams and needs to send the generated document as HTML.

interview.question: What does resumeAndPrerender do?
interview.answer: It continues a prerender that was previously aborted or postponed. It returns a Promise whose result includes prelude, a Web Stream containing static HTML, and possibly another postponed state.
interview.followUp: How would you stream the result in Node.js? Use resumeAndPrerenderToNodeStream instead, because this API returns a Web Stream.

interview.question: When should you use this API?
interview.answer: Use it for static server-side generation when all data should be ready before the result resolves. It can continue a previous prerender and produce complete static HTML.
interview.followUp: What API should be used when content must stream as data becomes available? Use a streaming SSR API such as renderToReadableStream.

interview.question: What inputs does it require?
interview.answer: The React node should represent the complete document, including the html element. The saved postponed state must come from a prerender API and be passed back unchanged.
interview.followUp: How does the generated document become interactive? Hydrate the server HTML on the client with hydrateRoot.

keyPoints: It continues an earlier React prerender and produces static HTML through a Web Stream.
Its main use is static server-side generation.
The promise waits for required data, including data used inside Suspense, before resolving.
Render the complete document from the React node, including the html element.
An interrupted render can continue with this API or switch to the resume streaming API.
gotchas: Use the Web Streams API version only where Web Streams are available. For Node.js, use the Node stream variant.
