Include every reactive value used by that factory in the dependency list so React can recreate the handle when those values change; in React 19, a function component receives ref as a prop.

parameters.name: ref
parameters.description: The ref received by the component; this is the ref whose exposed value will be customized.

parameters.name: createHandle
parameters.description: A zero-argument function that returns the value to expose through the ref.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline, constant-length list of all reactive values used by createHandle.

example.title: Expose a restricted input API
example.explanation: The child keeps its DOM ref private while exposing only focus and clear methods to the parent.

useCases.title: Expose selected input actions
useCases.scenario: A parent needs to focus, select, scroll, or clear a child-controlled input without owning its DOM node.

useCases.title: Hide implementation details
useCases.scenario: A component wraps a complex widget but should reveal only a small command API.

useCases.title: Bridge imperative APIs
useCases.scenario: A child must provide an imperative operation that cannot be expressed naturally with declarative props.

useCases.title: Publish reactive methods
useCases.scenario: A ref handle depends on current props or state and must be refreshed when those values change.

interview.question: What problem does useImperativeHandle solve?
interview.answer: It customizes the value exposed through a ref. The factory returns the handle, which can be any type and is often an object containing a small set of methods.
interview.followUp: Why use it instead of exposing a DOM node? A custom handle limits the parent to intentional operations and keeps the DOM implementation private.

interview.question: How should dependencies be specified?
interview.answer: The dependency list contains every reactive value read by the factory, including props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component. React compares dependencies with Object.is and recreates the handle when one changes or when no list is supplied.
interview.followUp: What constraint applies to the list? It must have a constant number of entries and be written inline.

interview.question: How is ref received in React 19?
interview.answer: In React 19, ref is available as a prop, so a function component can pass that prop directly to useImperativeHandle. The Hook returns undefined and must be called at the component’s top level.
interview.followUp: How would this differ in older React code? Components commonly used forwardRef to receive the ref, but React 19 documents ref as a prop.

keyPoints: It replaces the default ref exposure with a deliberately chosen handle.
Call it unconditionally at the component’s top level, not inside branches or loops.
The factory accepts no arguments and returns the complete exposed value.
The exposed handle is not restricted to an object; it may use any value type.
A compact methods object is the usual way to provide a narrow imperative API.
Dependency changes are detected with Object.is semantics.
gotchas: Keep the dependency array inline and fixed-length; it is not a dynamically sized list.
Do not omit reactive props, state, or component-local variables referenced by the factory.

useInsertionEffect.summary: useInsertionEffect lets CSS-in-JS libraries insert styles before layout effects run. It is a specialized client-side hook, not a general replacement for useEffect or useLayoutEffect.
useInsertionEffect.explanation: useInsertionEffect runs an effect setup when a component is added, before layout effects run, and repeats cleanup followed by setup when dependencies change. It is intended for CSS-in-JS libraries that must inject styles early; its cleanup runs when the component is removed.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Effect logic; it may optionally return a cleanup function.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional list of every reactive value referenced by setup, including props, state, and component-body declarations.

example.title: Inject a CSS rule
example.explanation: This component adds a CSS rule before layout effects and removes the corresponding style element during cleanup.

useCases.title: Inject generated styles
useCases.scenario: A CSS-in-JS library creates or updates a style element when generated rules change.

useCases.title: Clean up injected rules
useCases.scenario: A styling library removes a previously inserted rule when its owning component unmounts or its rule changes.

interview.question: What problem does useInsertionEffect solve?
interview.answer: It is a specialized effect for CSS-in-JS libraries. React runs its setup before layout effects, allowing styles to be inserted before effects that may measure layout.
interview.followUp: Why should ordinary components usually avoid it? Use useEffect or useLayoutEffect instead unless the code is implementing a CSS-in-JS library that needs this insertion point.

interview.question: Describe its cleanup lifecycle.
interview.answer: The setup function may return cleanup. On dependency changes, React runs cleanup with the old values and then setup with the new values; on unmount, it runs cleanup.
interview.followUp: What must the dependency list contain? Every reactive value referenced by setup, including props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component body.

interview.question: What constraints apply while the hook runs?
interview.answer: It returns undefined and runs only on the client. It cannot update state, refs are not attached yet, and DOM update timing should not be assumed.
interview.followUp: How should server-rendered CSS be handled? The documentation only establishes that this effect does not run during server rendering, so CSS-in-JS code must not depend on this hook for server output.

keyPoints: Reserve this hook for CSS-in-JS library implementation rather than normal application logic.
For most application code, choose useEffect or useLayoutEffect instead.
Use it to place style insertion ahead of layout-sensitive effects.
Initial setup occurs after mounting and before layout effects.
Changed dependencies cause cleanup with old values before new setup runs.
Unmounting invokes the cleanup returned by setup.
gotchas: Do not update state from this hook.
Refs are unavailable when the hook executes.
Do not assume that the DOM has already been updated.
The hook does not run during server rendering.

useLayoutEffect.summary: useLayoutEffect runs before the browser repaints, making it suitable for layout reads and visual corrections that must not flicker. Prefer useEffect unless the work must happen before paint.
useLayoutEffect.explanation: useLayoutEffect runs after React commits DOM changes but before the browser repaints. Use it when a visual effect must synchronously read layout and possibly update state before the user sees the result; otherwise prefer useEffect.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Function containing the effect logic; it may optionally return a cleanup function.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline list of reactive values referenced by setup.

example.title: Measure a tooltip before paint
example.explanation: Measures the tooltip before the browser paints, allowing its position to use the measured height without a visible intermediate layout.

useCases.title: Measure and position visual elements
useCases.scenario: A tooltip or popover needs its DOM dimensions to calculate a position before becoming visible.

useCases.title: Synchronize rendering with DOM geometry
useCases.scenario: A component must read an element's bounding box immediately after commit and use it to render a corrected layout.

useCases.title: Coordinate layout-sensitive integrations
useCases.scenario: An external visual system requires setup and teardown that must occur before repaint.

interview.question: What distinguishes useLayoutEffect from useEffect?
interview.answer: useLayoutEffect is the layout-sensitive counterpart to useEffect. It runs before the browser repaints, so it can measure DOM layout and update state before the user sees the result.
interview.followUp: When should useEffect be preferred? Prefer it for ordinary side effects, because useLayoutEffect blocks painting and can make the app slower.

interview.question: How do setup and dependencies control this Hook?
interview.answer: The setup function contains the effect logic and may return cleanup logic. The optional dependency list contains reactive values referenced by setup; React reruns the effect when those dependencies change.
interview.followUp: What should the dependency list look like? It should have a constant number of items and be written inline, such as [dep1, dep2].

interview.question: What server-rendering limitation applies?
interview.answer: Effects run only on the client, not during server rendering. Therefore, layout measurements must happen after the component is available in the browser.
interview.followUp: What alternative avoids blocking the initial paint? Replace useLayoutEffect with useEffect when an initial visual adjustment does not need to happen before paint.

keyPoints: Use it for visual work that must finish before paint, such as measuring or positioning an element.
A common pattern is to read an element's geometry, store the result in state, and render using that measurement.
Return cleanup code when the effect subscribes, attaches listeners, or otherwise needs to undo external work.
Include every reactive value used by setup in the dependency list so the measurement or synchronization stays current.
Use the Hook for its side effects; it does not produce a value for the component to consume.
gotchas: Call the Hook only at the top level of a component or custom Hook; move conditional behavior into the effect or extract a component.
Do not depend on this Hook for server-rendered measurements or other server-side effects.
Because its code and state updates block repainting, reserve it for effects that genuinely need to run before paint.

useMemo.summary: useMemo caches the result of a calculation between component renders. React reuses that result while its dependencies remain unchanged and recalculates it when they change.
useMemo.explanation: Call useMemo at the top level with a pure, argument-free calculation and an inline dependency list. React returns the cached result when every dependency is unchanged by Object.is; otherwise it runs the calculation again and stores the new result.

parameters.name: calculateValue
parameters.description: A pure, argument-free function that computes the value to cache; React calls it during the initial render and when dependencies change.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: An inline list containing every reactive value used by calculateValue; it must contain a constant number of items.

useMemo.returns: The cached calculation result, or a newly computed result when dependencies change.

example.title: Cache a derived list
example.explanation: The filtered array is reused when neither todos nor tab changes.

useCases.title: Skip expensive recalculations
useCases.scenario: A component repeatedly renders while an expensive derived value has unchanged inputs.

useCases.title: Preserve stable references
useCases.scenario: A memoized child needs a stable derived object or array so unchanged props can remain referentially equal.

useCases.title: Cache client-component computations
useCases.scenario: A client component needs to retain an expensive computation across its renders.

interview.question: What does useMemo do?
interview.answer: useMemo caches a calculation result between renders. React compares the dependency entries with their previous values using Object.is; unchanged dependencies reuse the prior value, while changed dependencies trigger recalculation.
interview.followUp: What must the calculation and dependency list look like? The calculation should be pure and take no arguments, and the list should include every reactive value it reads with a constant inline shape.

interview.question: Where may useMemo be called?
interview.answer: Call it at the top level of a component or custom Hook, never inside a loop or condition. Its purpose is to cache a computed value, not to perform side effects.
interview.followUp: How should conditional computation be structured? Extract a component or custom Hook so the Hook call remains unconditional at the top level.

interview.question: How do you choose dependencies?
interview.answer: The dependency list must contain every value from the component used by the calculation, including props, state, and locally declared variables or functions. React uses that list to decide whether the cached value remains valid.
interview.followUp: What happens when a dependency is omitted? React may reuse a stale result because the change is invisible to the dependency comparison.

keyPoints: It memoizes a computed value so later renders can reuse it.
The calculation receives no arguments, has no side effects, and returns the value to cache.
When every dependency is Object.is-equal to its previous value, React returns the existing cached value.
Any changed dependency invalidates the cache and causes the calculation to execute again.
Dependencies should cover all reactive values referenced by the calculation.
gotchas: Do not call useMemo inside loops or conditions; move conditional logic into a separate component or Hook.
Keep the dependency array inline with a fixed number of entries; include every reactive value used by the calculation.

useOptimistic.summary: useOptimistic lets a component display temporary optimistic state while an Action is pending. After the Action finishes or errors, React returns to the source value.
useOptimistic.explanation: useOptimistic creates temporary UI state for an in-progress Action. React displays the optimistic value during the Action, then uses the source value again after the Action finishes or fails.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value used when no Action is pending and after the optimistic Action is complete.

parameters.name: reducer
parameters.description: Optional pure function receiving the current optimistic state and an action, returning the next optimistic state.

useOptimistic.returns: An array containing optimisticState and set. optimisticState is the value or reducer-derived temporary state; set updates it inside an Action.

example.title: Optimistic like count
example.explanation: The count changes immediately during the Action and returns to the source value when the Action completes.

useCases.title: Instant mutation feedback
useCases.scenario: A user submits a form or mutation and the UI should reflect the expected result immediately.

useCases.title: Responsive controls
useCases.scenario: A network-backed control needs a temporary count, label, or status while its request is pending.

useCases.title: Optimistic list updates
useCases.scenario: A list item should appear or change immediately while the server operation completes.

interview.question: What does useOptimistic return?
interview.answer: useOptimistic returns exactly two values: the current optimistic state and a setter. Without a pending Action, the state equals the value argument; during an Action, it reflects the reducer result or the setter value.
interview.followUp: How should a reducer be designed? Keep it pure, accept the current state and action, and return the next optimistic state without side effects.

interview.question: What are the arguments to useOptimistic?
interview.answer: The first argument is the fallback value shown when no Action is pending. The optional reducer describes how an optimistic update transforms current state in response to an action.
interview.followUp: What happens after the Action completes? React goes back to rendering the value supplied as the first argument.

interview.question: How do you apply an optimistic update safely?
interview.answer: The setter must run inside an Action, commonly inside startTransition. React then re-renders with the optimistic value while the asynchronous work is pending.
interview.followUp: What if the setter runs outside an Action? React warns, and the optimistic state only renders briefly before the source value is used again.

keyPoints: Use it when the interface should show an expected result before background work finishes.
The Hook returns a state value and a function for requesting an optimistic value.
The first argument is the authoritative value displayed when no Action is pending.
The first returned item is the state currently rendered by the component.
The second returned item schedules the temporary state used during an Action.
Calling the setter in an Action immediately re-renders the UI with the requested optimistic state.
gotchas: Call the setter within an Action, such as the callback passed to startTransition; otherwise React warns and the optimistic rendering is only temporary.
A reducer must be pure and derive the next optimistic state only from its arguments.
Like other Hooks, call useOptimistic at component top level rather than inside conditions or loops.

useReducer.summary: useReducer lets a component manage state with a reducer. You dispatch actions, and the reducer returns the next state.
useReducer.explanation: useReducer stores state and gives you a dispatch function. Dispatch sends an action to a pure reducer, which returns the next state. React then renders the component again with that state.

parameters.name: reducer
parameters.description: A pure function that receives the current state and an action, then returns the next state.

parameters.name: initialArg
parameters.description: The value used directly as initial state, or passed to init.

parameters.name: init
parameters.description: Optional function that receives initialArg and returns the initial state.

useReducer.returns: An array containing the current state and a dispatch function. dispatch takes one action and has no return value.

example.title: A counter with useReducer
example.explanation: The button sends an action. The reducer returns a new state, and React renders the new count.

useCases.title: Centralize update logic
useCases.scenario: Several event handlers update the same state object or array.

useCases.title: Model user actions
useCases.scenario: State transitions need named actions such as added, changed, or deleted.

useCases.title: Initialize state once
useCases.scenario: Initial state requires expensive calculation or input data.

useCases.title: Combine with context
useCases.scenario: Many child components need shared state and dispatch.

interview.question: What does useReducer return, and how does dispatch work?
interview.answer: useReducer returns the current state and a dispatch function. Calling dispatch sends an action to the reducer, and React uses the reducer's returned value as the next state.
interview.followUp: When should the reducer throw? It can throw for an unknown action so missing update logic is detected instead of silently ignored.

interview.question: What rules should a reducer follow?
interview.answer: The reducer receives state and action and must return the next state. It should be pure, so it should not change objects or arrays already stored in state.
interview.followUp: How do you update an object? Return a new object, commonly with object spread, rather than assigning to a field on the old object.

interview.question: How can you avoid recreating initial state?
interview.answer: Pass the initial value as the second argument when it is already available. Pass an initializer function as the third argument when React should calculate the initial state from initialArg during initialization.
interview.followUp: Why use an initializer for expensive setup? It avoids calling the setup function again on later renders.

keyPoints: Call the Hook at the top level of a component or custom Hook, not inside a loop or condition.
The reducer defines how each action changes state.
Actions often use a type field and include only the data needed for the update.
React calls the reducer with the current state and dispatched action.
React usually groups updates from one event before updating the screen.
The optional third argument can calculate the initial state from initialArg.
gotchas: Reading state immediately after dispatch still gives the value from the current render.
Do not mutate state. Return a new object or array from the reducer.
In development Strict Mode, reducer and initializer calls can happen twice. Keep both functions pure.
Returning the same state value can cause React to skip the component and child re-render.

useSyncExternalStore.summary: useSyncExternalStore lets a component read from and subscribe to an external store. It supports server rendering through an optional server snapshot and re-renders when the snapshot changes.
useSyncExternalStore.explanation: Call this Hook at the component’s top level with a subscription function and a snapshot reader. React invokes the reader after store notifications, compares snapshots, and re-renders when the value changes; an optional third function supplies the server and hydration snapshot.

parameters.name: subscribe
parameters.description: Subscribes to the store with a callback and returns a cleanup function that unsubscribes.

parameters.name: getSnapshot
parameters.description: Returns the immutable snapshot needed by the component; unchanged store state must produce the same value.

parameters.name: getServerSnapshot
parameters.description: Optional initial snapshot used during server rendering and hydration; it must match between server and client.

useSyncExternalStore.returns: The current snapshot of the external store.

example.title: Subscribe to browser online status
example.explanation: Reads browser connectivity through a stable subscription and supplies a server fallback for hydration.

useCases.title: External state libraries
useCases.scenario: A state-management library exposes data outside React and needs concurrent-safe React integration.

useCases.title: Browser subscriptions
useCases.scenario: A browser API such as online/offline status changes independently of React state.

useCases.title: SSR and hydration
useCases.scenario: A server-rendered component reads external data that must match during hydration.

interview.question: How does useSyncExternalStore detect external-store changes?
interview.answer: The Hook connects React to a store outside React. subscribe registers a callback and returns cleanup, while getSnapshot reads the data; React calls getSnapshot after notifications and re-renders when its result changes by Object.is.
interview.followUp: Why must snapshots be cached? Repeated reads must return the same value when the store is unchanged, so a new object on every read can trigger endless updates.

interview.question: What contract does subscribe implement?
interview.answer: subscribe receives React’s callback and must invoke it whenever the store changes. It must also return a cleanup function that removes the subscription.
interview.followUp: What if subscribe changes identity between renders? React resubscribes using the new function, so define stable subscription logic when possible.

interview.question: When is getServerSnapshot required?
interview.answer: getServerSnapshot supplies the initial store value during server rendering and client hydration. The server and client values must match, commonly by serializing the server value for the client.
interview.followUp: What happens without it in SSR? Rendering the component on the server throws an error.

keyPoints: Use it to read data managed outside React while letting React coordinate subscription updates.
Invoke the Hook at component top level, not inside conditions, loops, or nested functions.
Implement subscribe as a registration operation whose returned cleanup reverses that registration.
Provide a reader for the portion of external-store state required by the component.
The store must notify React through the callback whenever its relevant data changes.
React uses Object.is semantics on snapshot results to decide whether the component needs another render.
gotchas: Return immutable snapshots. For mutable underlying data, create a new immutable snapshot only when the store changes; otherwise reuse the cached snapshot.
Cache the snapshot while the store is unchanged; unstable results can cause unnecessary work or an infinite update loop.
When server rendering, provide a third argument whose result matches the client’s initial snapshot during hydration.
Server-rendered components need getServerSnapshot; omitting it causes server rendering to fail.

useTransition.summary: useTransition lets a component mark non-urgent state updates as background Transitions. It returns a pending flag and a function for starting them.
useTransition.explanation: Call this Hook at component level to obtain a pending indicator and a function for marking state updates as Transitions. The callback runs immediately; synchronous updates inside it receive transition priority, while async work in React 19 can keep the pending state active and requires wrapping post-await state updates in another transition.
useTransition.returns: An array containing [isPending, startTransition]. isPending is a boolean indicating whether a Transition is pending; startTransition is a function that marks updates in its callback as Transitions.

example.title: Pending tab transition
example.explanation: Marks tab navigation as non-urgent and displays feedback while its transition is pending.

useCases.title: Non-blocking navigation
useCases.scenario: Keep tab, route, or panel navigation responsive while rendering the newly selected view.

useCases.title: Pending feedback
useCases.scenario: Show a spinner or disabled state while a Transition is still in progress.

useCases.title: Async updates
useCases.scenario: Run React 19 async Actions that coordinate requests and pending UI.

interview.question: What does useTransition return?
interview.answer: useTransition returns exactly two values: isPending and startTransition. The flag indicates whether a Transition is pending, and the function marks updates performed by its callback as Transitions.
interview.followUp: What should code outside a component use? Use the standalone startTransition function, but it does not provide an isPending indicator.

interview.question: Where and how is useTransition called?
interview.answer: Call useTransition at the top level of a component or custom Hook. It takes no parameters and returns the pending flag plus the transition-starting function.
interview.followUp: Why not call it conditionally? Hooks must follow React's top-level calling rules, so conditional calls would break Hook ordering.

interview.question: How does useTransition handle asynchronous Actions?
interview.answer: In React 19, startTransition can receive an async function. React sets isPending while the async transition is active; state updates after an await must be wrapped in another startTransition.
interview.followUp: What happens to urgent interaction updates? They can interrupt non-urgent transition work, keeping interactions responsive.

keyPoints: It lets React render selected UI work in the background rather than treating it as urgent.
Invoke it at component top level to obtain transition controls.
The Hook has no input arguments.
Its result is a two-item array containing the pending flag and transition function.
Use isPending to show feedback while transition work remains pending.
Wrap non-urgent state updates with startTransition.
The callback executes immediately, and synchronous state updates during it are marked as transition work.
gotchas: State updates after an async request need another startTransition wrapper.
Do not call the Hook outside a component or custom Hook; use standalone startTransition elsewhere.
The state update must occur during the callback, not later in a timer or unrelated callback.

version.summary: React lets you build web and native user interfaces from components. Components are JavaScript functions that can be combined into complete screens, pages, and apps.
version.explanation: React components are JavaScript functions that return user-interface markup. You can build larger screens and applications by combining smaller components, and use normal JavaScript such as conditions and array methods inside them.

example.title: A component made from other components
example.explanation: This component combines smaller components and data into one user-interface section.

useCases.title: Compose screens
useCases.scenario: Build a page from reusable interface pieces.

useCases.title: Render conditionally
useCases.scenario: Show different content based on application data.

useCases.title: Display lists
useCases.scenario: Render repeated interface elements from an array.

interview.question: What is a React component?
interview.answer: React components are JavaScript functions that return markup. Smaller components can be combined to create screens, pages, and applications.
interview.followUp: How can a component render a list? Use JavaScript array methods such as map() to produce the repeated markup.

interview.question: How does the example pass data into a component?
interview.answer: A component can receive data through its function parameters. The example receives a video object and passes it to child components and uses its fields in the returned markup.
interview.followUp: Why pass data to child components? It lets each child use the data it needs while keeping the larger interface composed from separate pieces.

interview.question: Why is component composition useful?
interview.answer: React lets developers combine components written by different people, teams, or organizations. This makes the same component model useful for both small projects and large applications.
interview.followUp: What is the benefit of this composition model? Independent components can be assembled into complete user-interface sections without changing how components are written.

keyPoints: React builds user interfaces from separate components.
Components can be combined to make complete screens, pages, and applications.
Use ordinary JavaScript if statements when content should appear only in certain conditions.
Use the array map() method to render items from a list.
gotchas: A component must follow JavaScript function rules. Use JavaScript conditions for conditional content and array methods such as map() for lists.

ViewTransition.summary: `<ViewTransition>` wraps a component tree and lets React animate its insertion, removal, updates, movement, or shared-element changes. It works with Transitions, Suspense, and `useDeferredValue`.
ViewTransition.explanation: ViewTransition wraps DOM content that React may animate during a Transition or Suspense update. React chooses enter, exit, update, or share based on what changed, then coordinates the browser View Transition API.
ViewTransition.syntax: <ViewTransition name={name} enter={enter} exit={exit} update={update} share={share} default={default} onEnter={onEnter} onExit={onExit} onShare={onShare} onUpdate={onUpdate}>{children}</ViewTransition>

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: A string or object name. Use it to match boundaries for shared-element transitions.

parameters.name: enter
parameters.description: CSS class, auto, none, or a transition-type map for insertion animations.

parameters.name: exit
parameters.description: CSS class, auto, none, or a transition-type map for removal animations.

parameters.name: update
parameters.description: CSS class, auto, none, or a transition-type map for content or layout changes.

parameters.name: default
parameters.description: Fallback animation choice when no specific transition type matches.

parameters.name: onEnter
parameters.description: Callback for an enter animation. It should return cleanup code.

parameters.name: onExit
parameters.description: Callback for an exit animation. It should return cleanup code.

parameters.name: onShare
parameters.description: Callback for a shared-element animation. It should return cleanup code.

parameters.name: onUpdate
parameters.description: Callback for an update animation. It should return cleanup code.

example.title: Animate enter and exit
example.explanation: The button changes state inside a Transition, so React can animate the element when it appears or disappears.

useCases.title: Animate enter and exit
useCases.scenario: A panel or item appears or disappears after a user action.

useCases.title: Animate a shared element
useCases.scenario: The same item moves between two rendered locations.

useCases.title: Animate Suspense reveals
useCases.scenario: A loading fallback changes into loaded content.

useCases.title: Use transition types
useCases.scenario: Different navigation directions need different CSS animations.

interview.question: How does React coordinate a ViewTransition?
interview.answer: ViewTransition wraps the DOM tree to animate. React assigns a view-transition name when the boundary participates and coordinates the browser transition itself.
interview.followUp: What happens if another React transition is already running? React waits for it to finish, and updates that arrive during it can be combined into the next animation.

interview.question: What animation triggers can ViewTransition detect?
interview.answer: Enter runs when the boundary is first inserted, exit when it is first removed, and update when React changes its DOM or its boundary moves or resizes. Share requires matching names in deleted and inserted subtrees.
interview.followUp: Which trigger has precedence for event callbacks? One event runs per boundary, and onShare takes precedence over onEnter and onExit.

interview.question: How do you customize a ViewTransition animation?
interview.answer: The enter, exit, update, and share props accept auto, none, a CSS class name, or an object keyed by transition type. React applies the selected class while the boundary animates.
interview.followUp: How can JavaScript control the animation? Use onEnter, onExit, onShare, or onUpdate, animate the supplied pseudo-elements with the Web Animations API, and return cleanup code.

keyPoints: Wrap the DOM content that should participate in a view transition.
An enter animation is selected when the boundary is newly inserted at the relevant position.
An update animation can run when React changes content inside the boundary or when the boundary moves or resizes.
A shared-element animation connects matching named boundaries across a removal and an insertion.
Without custom styling, the browser's default view transition is used.
gotchas: Use name only when matching an element removed from one subtree with an element added in another. React creates unique names for other animations.
A normal state update does not start this animation. Put the update in startTransition, or use Suspense or useDeferredValue.
For enter and exit, place ViewTransition before other DOM nodes in its parent output.
Use the prefers-reduced-motion media query to disable or reduce motion for users who request it.
